metadata.file_name: 39. Zheng et al. (2025). Unfolding key factors of resilience in ICT cognitive-motivational engagement: Global evidence from machine learning techniques.pdf
metadata.title: Unfolding key factors of resilience in ICT cognitive-motivational engagement: Global evidence from machine learning techniques

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 microdata and constructs a student-level binary outcome (resilient vs non-resilient in ICT engagement) by merging student, teacher, and school background files. The analytic sample is restricted to students with ESCS in the bottom quarter within their country/economy and with ICT engagement in the top quarter across the 53 participating countries/economies. The manuscript does not report applying PISA sampling weights or replicate weights (e.g., BRR/jackknife) in the machine-learning training/evaluation pipeline; instead, it describes standard ML preprocessing (kNN imputation, min–max normalization, and SMOTETomek) and ten-fold cross-validation. Because the paper does not specify weight variables (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or complex-survey variance estimation, readers should treat the results as model-based classification performance rather than fully design-weighted population estimates.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not applicable because the dependent variable is a binary classification derived from ICT engagement questionnaire responses (Likert-scale items aggregated into constructs), not a PV-based cognitive achievement score. Missing data handling is explicitly described via k-nearest neighbor (kNN) imputation, so the missing-data strategy is not a reporting gap.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2018 students from the 53 countries/economies that administered the optional ICT familiarity questionnaire. Defined ESCS-disadvantaged students as those in the bottom quarter of ESCS within each country/economy (n=68,959). Then classified resilience in ICT engagement as ICT engagement in the top quarter across the 53 countries/economies, yielding 13,418 ICT engagement resilient students (IRS) and 55,541 non-ICT engagement resilient students (NRS). The ML pipeline further applied kNN imputation for missing values, min–max normalization to [0,1], and SMOTETomek resampling to address class imbalance before training/testing within ten-fold cross-validation.

confounders_identified.variable_name: Ability to adapt to new situations

main_findings.target_variable: Resilience in ICT engagement (IRS vs NRS)
main_findings.performance_metrics: SVM (best by F-measure): AUC=95.10%, Accuracy=86.45%, Recall=97.09%, Precision=80.27%, F-measure=87.78% (10-fold cross-validation). RF: AUC=94.81%, Accuracy=86.86%, Recall=84.67%, Precision=88.18%, F-measure=84.70%. DT: AUC=84.84%, Accuracy=76.57%, Recall=75.19%, Precision=76.67%, F-measure=75.07%. LR: AUC=74.05%, Accuracy=68.13%, Recall=72.29%, Precision=67.14%, F-measure=69.51%.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 ICT familiarity questionnaire the study leveraged ENTUSE, ICTRES, RESILIENCE, EMOSUPS, and ST004D01T to classify resilience in ICT engagement (IRS vs NRS), finding that SVM achieved the highest overall discrimination (F-measure=87.78%) while LR was weakest (F-measure=69.51%). This indicates that strengthening students’ out-of-school ICT engagement for entertainment alongside self-efficacy and emotional parental support may help identify and support ESCS-disadvantaged students who can adapt and remain highly engaged in ICT, though the cross-sectional design and lack of reported survey-weighted estimation limit causal interpretation.

data.outcome_summary: The study uses PISA 2018 data from 53 countries/economies that administered the optional ICT familiarity questionnaire to classify students as ICT engagement resilient (IRS) versus non-resilient (NRS). Resilience is defined as ESCS in the bottom quarter within each country/economy combined with ICT engagement in the top quarter across the 53 economies, yielding 68,959 students (13,418 IRS; 55,541 NRS). After kNN imputation, min–max normalization, and SMOTETomek resampling for class imbalance, four supervised ML classifiers were compared using ten-fold cross-validation. SVM performed best overall with AUC=95.10%, Accuracy=86.45%, Recall=97.09%, Precision=80.27%, and F-measure=87.78%, outperforming RF (F-measure=84.70%) and substantially outperforming DT and LR. Key discriminators included ICT use outside school for entertainment (ENTUSE), ICT resources at home (ICTRES), self-efficacy (RESILIENCE), and parents’ emotional support (EMOSUPS). The paper does not report design-weighted estimation, and the outcome is a binary classification from questionnaire constructs, so results should be interpreted as predictive associations rather than causal effects.
